name: Pansy Purple
lede: Pansy purple is a flower name from the early nineteenth century, one of the purples that the Scottish painter Patrick Syme added when he revised Abraham Werner's color nomenclature.

sections.title: Syme's flower names
sections.body:
Werner's *Nomenclature of Colours*, a standard for describing minerals, plants and animals, was revised by Patrick Syme in 1814 and again in 1821 [1]. Syme added two principal colors, purple and orange, and renamed violet blue and plum blue as violet purple and plum purple [1]. As a painter who knew flowers, he also added names such as pansy purple and auricula purple, and he raised the total from Werner's list to 108 colors, then 110 in 1821 [1].

In Syme's purples, pansy purple follows violet purple and comes before campanula purple, imperial purple, auricula purple and plum purple [2]. His recipe for it mixes indigo blue with some carmine red and a faint touch of black [3]. That is a dark, blue-leaning purple, which is not what the screen swatch shows.

The chart numbers the color 38 among the purples, and its example objects are the sweet-scented violet, a mineral called Derbyshire spar and a beetle [4]. The flower in that list is the [[flower:violet|sweet violet]], not the garden pansy.

sections.title: Same name, different purples
sections.body:
The swatch here, a deep red-purple, is closer to the later plate of Robert Ridgway's 1912 color atlas than to Syme's [4]. Syme's own aged swatch reads as a dark bluish grey-purple today, while Ridgway's plate reads as a wine red, and the three are quite far apart [4]. The ISCC-NBS system of 1955 files the color in block 259 with neighbors named aster purple, beetroot purple and garnet lake, and Maerz and Paul record the name in 1814 [4].

Later books keep the idea but not the dye recipe. Baty reproduces a botany book of 1832 in which the petals of the sweet violet stand for this color, and a nineteenth-century entomology book where a small beetle's back does the same [3]. The name has always pointed at a range, not at a single point.

Nearby names in our data include [[violet-purple]], [[auricula-purple]], [[plum-purple]] and [[imperial-purple]] [2][4].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body:
This is one of the rarest named colors in our painting archive. Only 2 of 23,781 paintings match it, and the within-painting lens finds it in a single picture, so it is rarer than 86 per cent of the named colors [5]. The earliest of the two is a painting from 1506 by Giovanni di Niccolò Mansueti, and these are photographs of aged, varnished paintings, so a match shows a look-alike hue and not a pigment [5].

In printed English the phrase first appears around 1820, rises fastest in the 1910s and peaks in the 1930s, though a Google Books count of a two-word phrase is thin and noisy [5].
